newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland can cut more, privatise faster -- OECD.
newsitem.headline: Finland can cut more, privatise faster -- OECD.

text.p: Rapid growth gives Finland room to cut state spending, lower the tax burden and fuel job creation, the OECD said.

The country could also speed up privatisations, induce pension funds to become more active on international capital markets and take more efficient measures to create jobs, said an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development report.
The report was originally scheduled for release on Monday but the embargo was lifted on Friday after information from the report was published ahead of schedule.
The OECD said wage and price inflation should remain modest at three percent and two percent respectively in 1998.
Finland should also maintain a vigilant view on inflation, the Paris-based think-tank said in the 100-page document.
"There is still scope for additional expenditure restraint at a time the economy is growing rapidly," the OECD said.
This would have two advantages: it would give room to reduce the relatively high tax burden to support job creation, and boost fiscal flexibility to help cushion any future downturn.

Forecasting economic growth rising by about four percent annually in 1997 and 1998, modest inflation, and unemployment falling to about 13.5 percent in 1998, the OECD was in line with Finland's official forecasts.

Privatisation of the state sector -- which currently makes up one-fifth of Finnish manufacturing -- could be speeded up, the OECD said: the state's stake in its capital represents 55 billion markka ($10 billion) or 10 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

On pensions, it noted far-reaching reforms Finland has already made, but said the ageing of the population would be pronounced in Finland, with the old age dependency ratio reaching 40 percent in 2030, against a 35 percent OECD average.

Spending by the occupational pension system would rise to about 13 percent of GDP by 2030 from eight percent now -- contributions would have to rise to almost 12 percent from about 8.5 percent now, it said citing its own simulation.
"The volume of financial assets held by pension funds would thus grow from 37 percent of GDP at present to 65 percent by the year 2030, followed by a gradual depletion," it said.
Citing a risk the ratio between assets and pension obligations may be eroded, it said it would be advisable for the government to set binding requirements for funding.
And with future generations perhaps less willing to support a pension system in its current design, it said changes producing a higher return on pension fund assets may help.
"To this end, pension fund managers could be induced to become more active participants in international capital markets and to compete on the basis of their returns," it said.

Citing the risk that Finland's collective wage-bargaining system may prompt higher wage awards in some competitive sectors to spread through the economy, the OECD said Finland should stay vigilant on inflation.
It also saw a potential dilemma ahead in monetary policy, with the markka one of the strongest currencies in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) since its entry in 1996.

The dilemma would be either in focussing on exchange-rate stability and risking undermining inflation control, or leaving the markka to appreciate in wider ERM bands, which could damage competitiveness, the OECD said.

On jobs, it repeated that steps the government has taken to boost work incentives do not look to be enough to reach its objective of halving unemployment by 1999. In particular it cited municipal benefits to supplement jobless support.

"Recipients of such benefits still experience limited financial incentives to move into regular employment," it said. "Moreover, the relatively narrow wage structure ... tends to discourage employment of low-skilled workers."

It said Finland should shift the emphasis in job creation schemes to on-the-job training courses, away from subsidised work in municial administrations, "which appear to crowd out regular employment".
